title: Confirming What Others Think Doesn't Mean You Agree With Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author distinguishes validation, which recognizes the value of what people do, from confirmation, which recognizes the importance of what they say and think. The central claim is that leaders who confirm others build a kind of trust that validation alone cannot. The move is to separate honoring a person's view of the world from endorsing it, so a leader can say 'what you're saying makes perfect sense' without conceding the point. Confirmation is then shown to create safety for candid dialogue, drawing people beneath the surface of a conversation. The piece ends by urging leaders to build confirming statements into everyday conversations as a simple habit with outsized relational payoff.
points: Validation honors contribution while confirmation honors voice, and the second is the under-practiced route to trust.
Confirming statements such as 'You seem fired up about this' legitimate the person without endorsing the opinion.
Showing respect for how someone sees the world is explicitly decoupled from agreeing with their position.
Confirmation creates the safe space in which conversations move from surface exchange to candid exploration.
Trust is described as rising or falling with every conversation, making confirmation a habit rather than an occasional gesture.
quotes: People want to be validated and confirmed by those who lead them. Whereas validation recognizes the value of what people do, highlighting their contribution and quality, confirmation underlines the importance of what they say and think.
Statements like, “You seem fired up about this,” “I can tell you’ve thought a lot about this,

This has obviously caused you to worry,” and “What you’re saying makes perfect sense,” all suggest to others that what they have espoused matters. This legitimates who they are, not the opinion they espouse.

Confirmation underscores the value of how others see the world without endorsing their worldview. By accepting another person’s view of themselves through what they say and think, we show them deep respect. In this way, we honor them without necessarily agreeing with their positions or views.
Confirming others not only honors them, but promotes true dialogue. Facilitating shared understanding is about creating a safe space where others can speak up and speak into the conversation.
Trust between leaders and team members is elevated or diminished with every conversation. Confirming what others say, think, and believe promotes a shared understanding that increases trust.

The idea of confirmation gets less attention than it should. Consider building it into your leadership conversations. Everyone covets being confirmed by those they respect. Leaders who make it a habit enjoy the benefits of deeper and more honest relationships.
